opening.title: Measure a named boundary before comparing numbers
keyPoints: Latency has a start and completion event
Throughput counts useful completions per interval
CPU time and elapsed time answer different questions
opening.narration: A benchmark number has little meaning until we know what happened inside its boundary. A request's latency might include waiting in a queue, parsing, computation, and delivery, while a kernel benchmark may time only one prepared loop. Throughput counts completed useful work over an elapsed interval. CPU time counts processor execution under the operating system's accounting rules. These are not interchangeable units of success. This chapter uses both actual timing mechanics and explicitly supplied observations. When we calculate a model result, we will label it as such rather than pretending that deterministic output is a measurement of this machine.

question.prompt: Why is comparing one system’s median computation time with another’s end-to-end p99 misleading?
question.answer: The timing boundaries and distribution statistics differ. The numbers describe different events and populations.

opening.title: Concurrent request durations are not the elapsed interval
keyPoints: Three requests overlap from 0 to 10 milliseconds
Each latency is 10 milliseconds
Three completions in 10 milliseconds give 300 per second
opening.narration: Our supplied observations describe three requests that all begin at zero and complete at ten milliseconds. Adding their durations produces thirty milliseconds of request time, but the observed wall interval is only ten. Dividing three by that actual interval gives three hundred completions per second. The incorrect serial assumption gives one hundred. The program prints both calculations and labels the sum-based one wrong. These are arithmetic over a stated fixture, not timings collected by the program. This distinction matters whenever requests overlap: throughput needs a completion count and an elapsed observation window, not the sum of individual response durations.

question.prompt: Why is the sum of these three latencies not a valid throughput denominator?
question.answer: The requests overlap. Their 30 milliseconds of combined request time occurred within a 10-millisecond wall interval.

opening.title: One average can hide very different users’ waits
keyPoints: Nine requests take 1 ms; one takes 91 ms
Mean is 10 ms while the median is 1 ms
Nearest-rank p95 is 91 ms for this small sample
opening.narration: This supplied sample has nine quick requests and one slow request. The total is one hundred milliseconds across ten observations, giving a mean of ten. After sorting, the lower central observation is one, and both middle observations are one, so the median is one. Under the nearest-rank percentile rule, the ninety-fifth percentile selects rank ten and is ninety-one. The output makes the long tail visible, but ten samples do not establish a reliable population tail estimate. A percentile needs a stated definition, sample count, and representative workload. Sorting a local vector is acceptable here because the fixture's original order is not needed later.

question.prompt: Does a p95 of 91 ms from ten supplied observations prove the real service’s p95 is 91 ms?
question.answer: No. It is the selected order statistic of this small fixture. Population inference needs enough representative measurements and uncertainty analysis.

code.model: Statistics over a fixed illustrative sample, not a live benchmark.

opening.title: CPU seconds can exceed elapsed seconds
keyPoints: A process may execute on several cores
Waiting contributes wall time without equal CPU time
State whether accounting covers one thread or the whole job
opening.narration: A four-thread computation can use roughly four CPU seconds during one second of elapsed time if all four run continuously on separate cores. That is not a broken clock; CPU time adds execution charged across threads. Conversely, a job can take two wall seconds while using only six-tenths of a CPU second because it waits for I/O or scheduling. The difference suggests where to investigate, but does not identify one cause by itself. Helper processes and kernel accounting boundaries can also matter. Record whether your number covers one thread, one process, or the complete multi-process job.

question.prompt: Is process CPU time greater than wall time automatically invalid?
question.answer: No. Multiple threads can accumulate CPU execution simultaneously on different cores. The accounting scope must be stated.

mechanism.title: A clock read has cost and a limited resolution
keyPoints: Use a monotonic clock for durations
Very short work can be smaller than clock granularity
Batch enough work without silently changing the workload
mechanism.narration: Civil time can be adjusted, so duration measurements should normally use a monotonic clock such as steady_clock. Even that clock has a finite resolution and reading it has overhead. If one operation is extremely short, a measured zero does not imply infinite speed; it may be below the clock's visible scale. Batching operations can enlarge the interval, but also changes cache reuse and amortizes setup. State whether that batch represents the actual requirement. Keep the clock outside the operation only when the boundary excludes its overhead, and compare repeated observations under documented conditions.

question.prompt: What are two reasons a tiny operation might report zero elapsed time?
question.answer: Clock resolution can be too coarse, or the intended work may have been optimized away. Check both measurement mechanics and observable results.

mechanism.title: A benchmark must make the intended work observable
keyPoints: Validate a result outside the timed interval
Do not discard the only output of the hot loop
Inspect implausible generated code rather than guessing
mechanism.narration: If a loop computes a result that the program never uses, an optimizing compiler may legally remove it. Timing the empty remainder does not measure the intended calculation. The source benchmark keeps a checksum and compares it with an independent formula after the timed interval. That verifies useful behavior without including verification time in that chosen boundary. Using volatile everywhere is not a general repair because it changes access semantics and may create a different workload. If a result looks implausibly fast, inspect the generated code, build options, input size, and timing boundary before announcing an optimization win.

question.prompt: Why should the correctness check use an independent formula when practical?
question.answer: It reduces the chance that the benchmark and its checker repeat the same defect, while establishing that the intended computation produced the required result.

mechanism.title: High utilization is not proof of useful progress
keyPoints: A spin loop can keep a core busy
A saturated dependency can leave other resources idle
Measure completions and wait time alongside utilization
mechanism.narration: A core at one hundred percent can be calculating useful results, spinning on a lock, or repeatedly handling irrelevant events. The utilization number alone cannot distinguish them. Likewise, low CPU use does not mean the service has spare end-to-end capacity: a serialized storage or network dependency may be saturated. Use utilization to guide a hypothesis, then connect it to completions, latency, and queue growth. If adding clients raises CPU use while throughput stays flat and latency rises, more admitted work may simply be increasing contention. The objective is useful completion under constraints, not the highest busy percentage.

question.prompt: What evidence would make high CPU utilization a warning rather than a success?
question.answer: Flat useful throughput together with rising latency, contention, or queue length suggests the busy CPU is not improving the service objective.

mechanism.title: Control comparisons without hiding variation
keyPoints: Record compiler flags, input, and machine context
Alternate comparison order where practical
Report spread and uncertainty instead of one favorite run
mechanism.narration: Running version A once on a cool idle machine and B once after background work begins is a weak comparison. Repeat representative runs, record relevant conditions, and alternate ordering when practical to reduce drift. Variation can come from frequency changes, cache state, page faults, scheduling, contention, and instrumentation. Repetition reveals spread but does not automatically remove bias. If an apparent improvement is smaller than the experiment's noise, the evidence is weak. A statistically clear difference can still be operationally unimportant, so report both uncertainty and the size of the effect relevant to users.

question.prompt: Why should you avoid reporting only the fastest run of the preferred version?
question.answer: It selects favorable noise and conceals the distribution. A comparison needs a consistent sampling and reporting policy for both versions.

closing.title: Keep setup in or out for a stated reason
keyPoints: Kernel timing may exclude allocation and input creation
End-to-end timing includes required setup and delivery
Both views can be useful if labeled consistently
closing.narration: An optimized index can answer one query quickly after expensive construction. Timing only the query answers one question; timing construction plus the workload answers another. Neither boundary is inherently dishonest if stated clearly, but comparing them as if they were the same is misleading. The chapter's checksum example constructs data before timing because it studies summation mechanics. A file-processing service must also measure reading, allocation, parsing, and final delivery when those are part of the user's wait. Preserve separate measurements if they help diagnose where total time goes, then judge the change against the real objective.

question.prompt: When is excluding index construction from a query benchmark reasonable?
question.answer: When the stated workload reuses an already-built index and the benchmark explicitly measures query cost. End-to-end amortization still needs separate evaluation.

closing.title: Write the measurement claim so someone can reproduce it
keyPoints: Name the workload and completion criterion
Name the timing and accounting boundaries
Separate measured values from calculated models
Include correctness evidence and limitations
closing.narration: A useful result might say that this build processed this many bounded records, produced this checksum, and completed within a distribution of elapsed times under these conditions. That statement is much stronger than calling an implementation fast. Keep fixture arithmetic, modeled ceilings, and actual clock observations visibly separate. The lecture programs printed fixed statistics because their inputs were supplied; the source timing program prints a duration that varies. In a review, ask whether another person could reproduce the build, input, measurement boundary, and correctness check. If not, improve the experiment before arguing over a small speed difference.

question.prompt: What does a deterministic printed timing-like number prove when its inputs are supplied constants?
question.answer: It proves the program calculated that model or fixture correctly. It does not measure the current machine’s performance.
